title: F7 – Competitive dynamics
source: Zusammenfassung von Session 5 „Business Strategy (Part 2/2): Competitive Dynamics“

blocks.text: Business strategies are dynamic: firms respond to rivals' actions. Competitive rivalry is the ongoing set of competitive actions and responses among firms manoeuvring for an advantageous position (Apple vs Samsung in smartphones).

Mutual interdependence: firms recognize that their strategies are not implemented in isolation from rivals' actions and responses. Competitive dynamics = the total set of actions and responses of all firms in a market.

Typical sequence: competitor analysis (market and resource similarity) → drivers of competitive behaviour (awareness, motivation, ability) → competitive rivalry (likelihood of attack and of response) → outcomes (market position, financial performance).
First-mover advantages exist mainly in fast-cycle markets; in slow-cycle markets it is often better to be a fast second.

Market similarity: overlap of markets between the focal firm and a competitor. Resource similarity: overlap in type and amount of resources. The higher both overlaps, the higher the rivalry – which is why Blue Ocean Strategy differentiates to escape competition.

Awareness: understanding competitors to “see them coming”. Established firms may not see new entrants because of a sudden change (new technology, new law), organizational routines that create blindness, or success that creates blindness and overconfidence.
Motivation: gain/loss analysis – but rivalry can also be personal, irrational or even pathological.
Ability: the resources and capabilities to attack or respond.
Attack = a move that affects competitors; response = the competitors' counter-move. First mover = the actor taking the initial competitive action.
Advantages: high market shares, secured customer loyalty, authenticity (“since 1905”). Research shows they appear in fast-moving markets (rapid technological change, short product life cycles).

Disadvantages: uncertain demand, costs of innovation and learning (trial and error), lower initial quality, risk of path dependency and routines that make the firm too “traditional”. No first-mover advantage in slow-cycle markets → second-mover advantage.

sections.heading: Interactive strategies on price and quality (D'Aveni)

blocks.text: Firms are positioned by price and perceived quality: D = differentiating business, M = mid-point business, L = cost-leading business, U = uncompetitive business. A value line links the price–quality combinations customers accept.
At time t, D improves its perceived quality while holding prices → customer expectations shift to a 2nd value line; M and L must improve quality or cut prices to stay on it.
At t+1, M lowers its price at constant quality → a 3rd value line; L and D must adapt. Competitive moves continuously shift the value line – yesterday's position becomes uncompetitive (U).

Slow-cycle markets: players are shielded from imitation for long periods and imitation is costly. Advantage from high barriers to entry (high fixed costs, complex processes, patents, history); slow responses (space industry).
Standard-cycle markets: in between – moderate imitation pressure; advantage from scale, market share and brand built over time.

Fast-cycle markets: little or short protection, cheap imitation, low barriers. Advantage from adaptation (exploration, awareness of competition, flexible production) and quickness of decision and implementation (smartphones, AI LLMs).
Ongoing set of competitive actions and responses among firms manoeuvring for an advantageous market position.
Firms recognize that their strategies depend on competitors' actions and responses.
Overlap of markets (market similarity) and of resources (resource similarity) between two firms.
Awareness, motivation and ability – the drivers of competitive behaviour.
The firm taking the initial competitive action in a market.

sections.heading: Further thinking: using F7 in the exam

blocks.text: To predict a rival's reaction, go through market similarity, resource similarity, awareness, motivation and ability – then conclude on the likelihood of response.

When a case discusses being first (first app, first smart ring), qualify the market velocity: in a fast-cycle market, speed and adaptation matter; in a slow-cycle market, being a fast second can be smarter.
